title: Identify Materials by Their Properties
seo_title: Grade 5 Properties of Materials Worksheets: Magnets, Conductors, Hardness, Solubility
standard_text: Make observations and measurements to identify materials based on their properties.
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 science worksheets on properties of materials (NGSS 5-PS1-3): hardness, shine, magnetism, electrical and thermal conductivity, solubility, mass and volume, and mystery-material tables. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Use properties as clues to identify a material.
key_sub: Test magnetism, conductivity, hardness and solubility, and measure mass and volume, until only one material fits every clue.
body_html:
How to think about it

A property is something you can observe or measure about a material. Every material has its own set of properties, so you can use them like clues to identify it.

  • Color and shine (reflectivity): you can see them.
  • Hardness: a harder material scratches a softer one.
  • Magnetism: iron and steel are attracted to a magnet. Many metals, like aluminum and copper, are not.
  • Conductivity: metals let electricity and heat move through them. Rubber, plastic, wood and glass are insulators.
  • Solubility: salt and sugar dissolve in water; sand does not.
  • Measurements: mass with a balance (g) and volume with a graduated cylinder (mL).

iron nailyesyesno
copper wirenoyesno
wooden sticknonono
saltnonoyes
Example

A mystery material conducts electricity but is not attracted to a magnet. Use the table above.

Conducts electricity: iron nail or copper wire.

Not attracted to a magnet: not the iron nail.

Answer: copper wire

Example

Water in a graduated cylinder is at 40 mL. A rock is dropped in and the water rises to 52 mL. What is the volume of the rock?

The rock pushes aside its own volume of water.

52 − 40 = 12.

Answer: 12 mL

Common mistakes

  • Thinking every metal sticks to a magnet. Only iron, steel and a few others do.
  • Using one clue when two materials share it. Keep testing until only one material fits all the clues.
  • Reading the water level after the object is in as the object's volume. Subtract the starting level.
  • Thinking only metals conduct electricity. Graphite (pencil lead) conducts too.

faq.q: What are the properties of materials?
faq.a: Properties are things you can observe or measure, such as color, hardness, shine, whether it is attracted to a magnet, whether it conducts electricity or heat, and whether it dissolves in water.
No. Iron and steel are attracted to magnets, but aluminum, copper, gold and silver are not. A US nickel coin is mostly copper, so it does not stick to a magnet.

faq.q: What is the difference between a conductor and an insulator?
faq.a: A conductor lets electricity or heat move through it easily, like copper or steel. An insulator slows it down, like rubber, plastic, wood or glass.

faq.q: How do you find the volume of a rock?
faq.a: Put water in a graduated cylinder, read the level, drop in the rock and read again. The difference is the rock’s volume in mL.

items.q: Sofia puts a rod in hot water and feels how fast the other end warms up. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's thermal conductivity.

items.q: Which property would best help you tell a piece of iron from a piece of aluminum that look the same?
c: whether it is attracted to a magnet
items.e: Both are shiny gray solid metals, but only iron is attracted to a magnet.

items.q: Ben drags a magnet through a pile of sand. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's response to magnets.

items.q: Hana stirs a powder into water to see if it disappears. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's solubility.

items.q: Which statement is true about properties?
c: Size is the only property that matters.
Different materials can be identified by their properties.
A property can only be found by tasting.
All metals have exactly the same properties.
items.e: Each material has its own set of properties. Testing several properties lets you identify it.

items.q: Noah puts a sample on a balance. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's mass.

items.q: Which tool is best for measuring the volume of a liquid?
items.e: A graduated cylinder has marks in milliliters (mL) for measuring liquid volume.

items.q: Which property describes whether a material dissolves in water?
items.e: A material that dissolves in water, like salt or sugar, is soluble in water.

items.q: Mia scratches a fingernail across a piece of gypsum. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's hardness.

items.q: What is a property of a material?
c: something you can observe or measure about it
items.e: Properties are things you can observe or measure, like color, hardness or whether it is attracted to a magnet.

items.q: A material that lets heat move through it quickly is called
items.e: Metals are good thermal conductors, so a metal spoon in hot soup gets hot quickly.

items.q: Which property describes how easily a material can be scratched?
items.e: Hardness tells how well a material resists being scratched. A harder material scratches a softer one.

items.q: Ethan tries to scratch a mineral with a steel nail. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's hardness.

items.q: A material that does not let electricity flow through it easily is called
items.e: Rubber, plastic and glass are insulators. Wires are covered in plastic or rubber to keep us safe.

items.q: A material that lets electricity flow through it easily is called
items.e: Metals like copper are good electrical conductors. That is why wires are made of copper.

items.q: Which property can you observe just by looking?
items.e: You can see color. To find conductivity, mass or solubility you need to test or measure.

items.q: Reflectivity describes how a material
c: reflects light, like a shiny mirror
items.e: A shiny metal spoon or a mirror has high reflectivity. A brick reflects very little light.

items.q: Why do pot handles often have plastic or wooden covers?
c: Plastic and wood are poor conductors of heat.
Plastic and wood make the pot heat faster.
items.e: Plastic and wood are thermal insulators. Heat moves through them slowly, so the handle stays cool enough to hold.

items.q: Chloe tries to scratch a mineral with a steel nail. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's hardness.

items.q: Which tool would you use to measure the mass of a mineral sample?
items.e: A balance measures mass in grams.

items.q: A cooler keeps drinks cold. What property should the walls of the cooler have?
c: They should be attracted to magnets.
They should be good electrical conductors.
They should be good thermal insulators.
items.e: Thermal insulators slow down the movement of heat into the cooler.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?
items.e: Metals conduct electricity. A cotton ball is an insulator.

items.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
items.e: A steel paper clip contains iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Many metals, like aluminum, copper and gold, are not.

items.q: Is every metal attracted to a magnet?
c: No metal is attracted to a magnet.
No. Iron and steel are, but metals like aluminum and copper are not.
items.e: Only some metals, mainly iron, steel, nickel and cobalt, are attracted to magnets. An aluminum can is not.

items.q: A mystery object conducts electricity but is not attracted to a magnet. What could it be?
items.e: Aluminum is a metal, so it conducts electricity, but it is not magnetic.

items.q: Which metal object will not stick to a magnet?
items.e: A silver spoon is a metal, but it has no iron in it, so a magnet does not attract it. Iron and steel are attracted to magnets.

items.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
items.e: A steel screw contains iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Many metals, like aluminum, copper and gold, are not.

items.q: Which object is an electrical insulator?
items.e: A paper cup does not let electricity flow through it. All the other objects are metals, which are conductors.

items.q: You tap two spoons on a hot pan. Which material would carry heat to your hand fastest?
items.e: Copper is one of the best thermal conductors, which is why some pots have copper bottoms.

items.q: A silver spoon, a wooden spoon and a plastic spoon are put in hot soup at the same time. Which handle feels warm first?
c: They all warm up at the same time.
items.e: Metal is a good thermal conductor, so heat moves up the silver spoon fastest. Wood and plastic are insulators.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?
items.e: Metals conduct electricity. A plastic straw is an insulator.

items.q: A steel spoon, a wooden spoon and a plastic spoon are put in hot cocoa at the same time. Which handle feels warm first?
c: They all warm up at the same time.
items.e: Metal is a good thermal conductor, so heat moves up the steel spoon fastest. Wood and plastic are insulators.

items.q: Which pair of objects are both conductors of electricity?
c: a wooden spoon and a paper towel
a plastic cup and a glass marble
a steel key and a copper penny
a rubber band and a steel key
items.e: Steel and copper are metals, and metals conduct electricity.

items.q: Pencil “lead” is really graphite. A student touches the wires of a circuit to the graphite and the bulb lights. What does this show?
items.e: Graphite is not a metal, but it conducts electricity. Testing is the only way to be sure.

items.q: A mystery object is attracted to a magnet. What else can you predict about it?
c: It probably conducts electricity, because it is likely iron or steel.
items.e: Objects attracted to magnets are usually iron or steel. These are metals, which conduct electricity.

items.q: A US nickel coin does not stick to a magnet. Why?
c: Coins cannot be tested with magnets.
It is made mostly of copper, which is not magnetic.
items.e: A US nickel is about three-fourths copper. There is not enough nickel in it to be attracted.

items.q: A silver spoon, a wooden spoon and a plastic spoon are put in hot tea at the same time. Which handle feels warm first?
c: They all warm up at the same time.
items.e: Metal is a good thermal conductor, so heat moves up the silver spoon fastest. Wood and plastic are insulators.

items.q: Which kitchen item works best as an oven mitt?
items.e: Cloth is a thermal insulator. Metals would let the heat through quickly.

items.q: Which metal object will not stick to a magnet?
items.e: Aluminum foil is a metal, but it has no iron in it, so a magnet does not attract it. Iron and steel are attracted to magnets.

items.q: Why are electrical wires made of copper covered with plastic?
c: Plastic conducts electricity better than copper.
Copper conducts electricity and plastic insulates it.
items.e: The copper carries the electricity. The plastic cover keeps the electricity from reaching your hand.

items.q: You stir sand into water and stir sugar into water. What do you observe?
c: The sand disappears; the sugar stays.
The sugar disappears; the sand stays visible and settles.
items.e: Sugar is soluble in water. Sand is not, so you can still see it.

items.q: A graduated cylinder holds 50 mL of water. When a marble is dropped in, the water rises to 66 mL. What is the volume of the marble?
items.e: The marble pushes aside its own volume of water: 66 − 50 = 16 mL (1 mL = 1 cubic centimeter).

items.q: A graduated cylinder holds 40 mL of water. When a toy car is dropped in, the water rises to 54 mL. What is the volume of the toy car?
items.e: The toy car pushes aside its own volume of water: 54 − 40 = 14 mL (1 mL = 1 cubic centimeter).

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Pepper does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Two clear liquids look the same. Which test would help tell water from vinegar?
c: Smell them, or add baking soda and look for fizzing.
items.e: Vinegar has a sharp smell and fizzes with baking soda. Water does neither. (Only smell by wafting the air toward you.)

items.q: A copper wire is placed in a cup on a balance. The cup alone has a mass of 5 g. The cup and the copper wire together have a mass of 98 g. What is the mass of the copper wire?
items.e: Subtract the mass of the cup: 98 − 5 = 93 g.

items.q: A cube of wood and a cube of steel are the same size. Which measurement will be different?
items.e: They take up the same space, so their volumes are equal, but the steel has more mass.

items.q: Which of these dissolves in water?
items.e: Drink mix powder dissolves: it breaks into particles too small to see and spreads through the water.

items.q: Which property helps you separate a mix of iron filings and sand?
c: Sand is attracted to a magnet.
Iron is attracted to a magnet.
items.e: A magnet pulls out the iron filings and leaves the sand behind.

items.q: A rock is placed in a cup on a balance. The cup alone has a mass of 10 g. The cup and the rock together have a mass of 98 g. What is the mass of the rock?
items.e: Subtract the mass of the cup: 98 − 10 = 88 g.

items.q: A copper wire is placed in a cup on a balance. The cup alone has a mass of 5 g. The cup and the copper wire together have a mass of 90 g. What is the mass of the copper wire?
items.e: Subtract the mass of the cup: 90 − 5 = 85 g.

items.q: Your fingernail can scratch talc and gypsum, but not calcite. What does this tell you?
c: Fingernails cannot be used to test hardness.
Calcite is the softest of the three.
Your fingernail is harder than talc and gypsum but softer than calcite.
items.e: Something that scratches a mineral is harder than it. Your fingernail is softer than calcite.

items.q: Which unit is used for the volume of a liquid?
items.e: Liquid volume is measured in milliliters or liters.

items.q: A student does a scratch test on three minerals: Feldspar scratches gypsum; Feldspar scratches talc. Which mineral is the hardest?
items.e: A harder mineral scratches a softer one. Feldspar is never scratched, so it is the hardest.

items.q: A graduated cylinder holds 50 mL of water. When a marble is dropped in, the water rises to 74 mL. What is the volume of the marble?
items.e: The marble pushes aside its own volume of water: 74 − 50 = 24 mL (1 mL = 1 cubic centimeter).

items.q: Which of these dissolves in water?
items.e: Salt dissolves: it breaks into particles too small to see and spreads through the water.

items.q: A mineral scratches glass. Glass cannot scratch the mineral. What can you say?
c: The mineral is harder than glass.
The mineral will dissolve in water.
items.e: The harder material makes the scratch.

items.q: A student does a scratch test on three minerals: Fluorite scratches calcite; Calcite scratches talc. Which mineral is the hardest?
items.e: A harder mineral scratches a softer one. Fluorite is never scratched, so it is the hardest.

items.q: A student does a scratch test on three minerals: Topaz scratches gypsum; Topaz scratches apatite. Which mineral is the hardest?
items.e: A harder mineral scratches a softer one. Topaz is never scratched, so it is the hardest.

items.q: Diamond is the hardest natural mineral. Which statement is true?
c: Diamond is attracted to a magnet.
Diamond can scratch every other mineral.
items.e: The hardest mineral scratches all softer ones, and nothing natural scratches it.

items.q: A jeweler wants to test if a gold ring is real without damaging it. Which test is best?
c: Check if it is attracted to a magnet (real gold is not).
items.e: Real gold is not magnetic. If a magnet pulls it, the ring has iron or steel in it.

items.q: Maya wants to find out which material is the best thermal insulator for a lunch box. What should she keep the same in her test?
c: only the color of the boxes
the starting temperature and amount of the food, and the time
items.e: Only the material should change. Everything else must stay the same for a fair test.

items.q: Two powders look the same. One fizzes with vinegar, and one does not. Why is this a useful test?
c: It shows the powders are different materials with different properties.
It shows they are the same material.
It shows they are both magnetic.
items.e: Different results on the same test mean different materials.

items.q: Leo tests 4 objects in a circuit. The bulb lights for a key, a foil ball and a coin, but not for a button. Which conclusion is best?
c: The key, foil and coin are conductors; the button is an insulator.
Only the button is a conductor.
items.e: Objects that let the bulb light are conductors. The button stops the electricity, so it is an insulator.

items.q: Students test which material keeps ice frozen longest: foil, wool or plastic wrap. The ice in wool lasts longest. What does this show?
c: Wool is the best conductor of heat.
Wool is the best thermal insulator of the three.
items.e: Wool slows the movement of heat from the air to the ice, so the ice melts more slowly.

items.q: A class wants to know which material makes the best wire for a circuit. Which property should they test?
items.e: A wire must carry electricity well, so test how well each material conducts.

items.q: Omar sorts 10 objects into “attracted to a magnet” and “not attracted.” Which conclusion is supported?
c: All attracted objects contain iron or steel, but not all metals are attracted.
items.e: Some metals, like aluminum and copper, end up in the “not attracted” group.

items.q: Noah tests whether salt dissolves faster in warm or cold water. Which plan is a fair test?
c: Use the same amount of salt and water in two cups, changing only the temperature.
Use different cups and different amounts.
Use more salt in the warm cup.
items.e: Change only one variable (temperature). Keep the salt, water and stirring the same.

items.e: Metals are usually shiny and good conductors of electricity and heat.

items.q: Ava finds a shiny gray rock that is attracted to a magnet. Which mineral could it be?
items.e: Magnetite contains a lot of iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Quartz, talc and calcite are not.
